name: TensorBase
workload: Round 1: synthetic aggregations (sum/max/complex-sum) over 1 trillion generated integers. Round 2: TPC-H-style analytical queries over NYC Taxi dataset (1.47B rows), measuring end-to-end scan bandwidth (GB/sec).
claimed_speedup: Synthetic: 1059x (sum), 1922x (max), 10833x (complex sum) vs ClickHouse. Real-world NYC Taxi: 4.5x-31x faster end-to-end; Q#2 bandwidth 81.4 GB/sec vs ClickHouse's 6.5 GB/sec.
hardware: 6-channel DDR4-2400 REG ECC DRAM, measured practical max bandwidth ~100 GB/sec via Intel VTune; exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Author's own blog acknowledges the synthetic 1T-row benchmark 'makes no sense for the real world' and is meant only to illustrate JIT-vs-volcano-model architectural differences, not a realistic workload.
caveats: First-party project blog (announcement post), not independent. Synthetic-benchmark ratios (>50x, up to 10833x) are implausible and self-acknowledged as non-representative; capped at tier C per hard rules. No CPU model or compiler/flags stated. Project inactive since May 2022 (>3 years), effectively abandoned.
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query 'TensorBase ClickHouse' -> tensorbase.io blog post 'Show HN: TensorBase: 5x~10000x Faster Drop-In/Accelerator for ClickHouse in Rust' (2021-03-16)

name: Modin
workload: Customer-segmentation-style groupby().apply() with a custom aggregation function, run with a mixed pandas/Modin approach on an unspecified-size dataset; also a broader 'heavy pandas operations' chart and a for-loop anti-pattern example on 10M rows x 10 columns.
claimed_speedup: ~7x faster than pandas for the groupby().apply() workload (author notes Modin only wins once a pandas op takes >5s; it lost in the for-loop anti-pattern example).
hardware: HP ZCentral 4R Workstation: Intel Xeon W-2245, 8 cores/16 threads, 64GB RAM
tradeoffs: Modin's own benchmark author states its implementation is only faster than pandas when the pandas operation already takes >5 seconds; a small/short-running or sequential for-loop workload was slower under Modin than plain pandas.
caveats: Blog is written by a Modin core contributor (first-party, not independent); dataset size, pandas/Modin versions, and Python version are not stated, so methodology is partial. Capped at tier C accordingly.
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query 'modin pandas' -> 'How to Parallelize Pandas with Modin' (dchigarev.github.io/modin_perf_examples), redirect page gh_page_1.html

name: Xorbits
workload: TPC-H queries at SF100 (~100GB) and SF1000 (~1TB) scale, run as a distributed pandas-API-compatible dataframe workload against DaskDF, Modin, and Koalas.
claimed_speedup: ~8x faster than DaskDF and ~4x faster than Modin on TPC-H SF100; at SF1000, Xorbits completed all queries while DaskDF, Koalas, and Modin 'stumbled on most'. Companion arXiv paper claims a 2.66x average speedup over the fastest state-of-the-art solution across its evaluation.
tradeoffs: Because the workload sizes (100GB-1TB) exceed single-node pandas memory, pandas itself is not directly benchmarked here (would OOM); the real comparison is against other distributed pandas-API frameworks (Dask/Modin/Koalas), not the pandas baseline itself.
caveats: baseline_in_list=false: pandas (the listed incumbent) can't run this scale so the direct comparison is to Dask/Modin/Koalas instead. Hardware/CPU not stated on the comparisons page. Companion paper (arXiv:2401.00865) numeric claim not confirmed to be peer-reviewed (checked abstract only); no exact CPU/cluster spec found in the fetched pages. Project last commit ~17 months ago (stale by wave criteria).
